specials.text: Scratched into the stone at the dead end: THE DEAD KEEP WHAT IS THEIRS.

captives.text: Two grave robbers are binding a struggling grave-digger.

specials.text: Old bones are heaped against the wall, picked clean.
A dead orc courier lies here, a satchel of orders under him. One names the Ruinfield Gate, and the countersign its garrison asks for.
The gate stands open. Cut into the lintel in the old script: HOLD UNTIL RELIEVED.

captives.text: A beastman deserter is chained in the stables, and two warbreed hounds are kept hungry beside him.

garrisons.text: Three old goblins stand to in the gatehouse, spears level, as if the war never ended.
Two orc guards hold the keep hall, their armor patched with twenty years of scrap.

specials.text: Nailed to the armory door: the last orders of Ashgate's commander, with the countersign the garrison was to accept from its relief.

garrisons.text: Ashgate's captain guards the archive himself, a guard at his side.

specials.text: Goats fill the yard, bellies swollen. In four months these pens will hold beastmen.
{pc} knows the smell of this place, though {pc} was born somewhere like it, not here.

captives.text: A slaver and two beastman troopers are dragging an old-breed goblin toward the cull rooms.

specials.text: Glass vats as tall as an orc line the hall. Most are cracked; something moved in the last whole one.
Under the laboratory bench, wrapped in oilcloth: the vat-master's working notes.
Bones fill the room to the knee: orcs and goblins of breeds no longer made.
Ledgers fill the shelves: every breed of orc and goblin the vats made, and the day each older breed was culled.
{pc} finds the orc lines. {pc}'s own breed is marked for the cull, the order signed but never carried out.
{pc} finds the goblin lines. {pc}'s breed is listed as a failure, kept for labor until a better one was ready.
In the officers' quarters, a brass token hangs on a hook by the door, waiting for whoever has the watch.
Records of the civil wars fill the map room: which lieutenant betrayed which, and when. Vael is in none of them as a traitor.

garrisons.text: Two clockwork servitors stand to beside their bunks, as they have every morning for twenty years.
A clockwork soldier guards the stair down to the command deck.

specials.text: Maps of a war that ended twenty years ago cover the walls, and someone still moves the pins each morning.
Orders in Vael's hand, dated every day for twenty years: hold the line, await the Dark Lord's word.
In the vault lies the Seal of Command, the Dark Lord's own, left with his most trusted lieutenant.

garrisons.text: The Iron Golem stands at the war room door, and turns its head.
Lieutenant Vael, an elf in a uniform twenty years old, bars the vault door. "You are not my relief," he says.

specials.text: The stockade is new timber over old stone. Fresh beastmen drill in the yard, none of them a year old.
Herd after herd of pregnant goats. Grisk has an army due within the year.
The crafter's writing desk holds a bound book: herbs, doses, and the words of the training.

captives.text: Two troopers keep the warlord's crafter at her work.

specials.text: A throne of old siege timber stands under the banners of three dead lieutenants.
Ember-red banners hang over the nave. The hymn painted on the wall asks the Dark Lord to come home, and promises him an army when he does.
A pilgrim's slate hangs by the vestry door, chalked with the words the guards on the Throne Road want to hear: "The night keeps faith."
Carts stand ready in the yard, loaded with shrouded bodies and pointed north.

captives.text: Faithful acolytes are loading the dead onto carts. An old orc woman screams at them to give her husband back.

specials.text: Niche after niche stands empty. The Lady's priests laid these dead to rest a hundred years ago; someone has taken every one.
Among the empty niches {pc} finds name-plates in the old tongue of the homeland: elders deported and buried here, and now taken too.
Shelves of deportation rolls, a thousand years of them. Somewhere here {pc} finds a family name they were told never to speak.
The breeding ledgers of the empire, shelf on shelf. Whole breeds of goblin are entered here and struck out in a single line.
A reading desk, still laid out for a clerk: ink, sand, and an order to the Saltgate dated the day the capital fell.

garrisons.text: Three clockwork scribes step out from the stacks and hold out their hands for your pass.

specials.text: On a Faithful clerk's desk lies the watchword they give the Citadel's bound: "The throne waits."

A spy's ledger of the alliance's plans against the Dark Lord: three hundred and twelve of them, each struck through as it failed, but one. That page has been cut out, long ago, with a very sharp knife.

garrisons.text: A clockwork soldier guards the sealed stacks, with two scribes behind it.

specials.text: Barracks for a thousand. The bunks are made, and the bound who keep them sleep in shifts beside the gate they have kept for twenty years.

garrisons.text: Bound orcs in the Dark Lord's livery fill the gate passage. "The watchword," their captain says.
A war-engine squats at the head of the stair down, and an orc captain stands at its shoulder.

specials.text: Petitions to the Dark Lord, ten deep on every table. The last are dated the day his will left the world. None was answered.
The Faithful have chalked the floor for a rite: a circle of the Lady's dead around an empty chair, and a name left blank.

captives.text: Faithful zealots stand over a chained Priest of Death. Their keeper turns: "She is for the rite. You are not."

specials.text: The Dark Lord's throne stands empty. Dust lies undisturbed on the seat, twenty years of it, and in the arm is set a gnome-made device that still hums, as if listening for something that never comes.
Wards are cut into every lintel, the same knot of lines over and over. They are fresh. Someone has been recutting them for a hundred years.
A ledger of the barrow-wardens lies open on a lectern, every name struck through but the last. The last has no date of death.
Mummified wardens stand in their niches, linen fresh and resin still tacky. They were wrapped by someone who meant them to get up again.
The air is cold enough to hurt. A voice like dry leaves says, from everywhere: "The wards hold. They will always hold. Lie down."

Mourncourt's great hall is swept and the candles lit, though the forest has grown through the windows. The portraits on the walls are all of one family, and none of them has aged across six hundred years of paint.
A chapel of the Lady, its altar overturned and its grey hangings slashed. It still feels like hers. The dead here sleep, and so might you.
A long table set for forty. The plates are clean. The cups are not.

captives.text: The house dead stand watch over a pale figure chained to a bed, who looks at you without hope.

specials.text: Coffins of black wood, each lined with earth from somewhere else. Most are empty, and the earth in them is warm.
The coffins in this vault are small.
The empire's cisterns watered the vat-farms of the Mire. The pumps stopped twenty years ago and the swamp came in.
Something big has been through the sluice hall. The iron grilles are bent outward, and the walls are scored in rows, many heads wide.
Ferry poles, a boat's ribs, and a goblin's boot lie along the ledge, all of it chewed.
Faded paint on the wall: FRINGE WATER BOARD. NO DRINKING FROM THE SETTLING TANKS.
Raider boss Krell kicks over a table of stolen tins. “That’s ours,” she says, and her gang draws steel.
The tanks are dry, but the air down here is cool and smells of rust and old rain.
Brass watchmen grind to life around the pump-house strongbox, and the drowned dead stand up behind them.
Someone has chalked a tally of the dead beside the valve wheels. The last mark is fresh.
The Pumpmaster’s gang holds the valve room, his rust-eaten sentinels clanking at his side.
Gnawed bones carpet the cistern lip. Most are rat. Some are not.
Hyena-folk feast in the cistern, and the rats that serve them pour out of the drains.
A brass plate reads: RESERVE OF LAST RESORT. TO BE OPENED BY THE WATERWARDEN ALONE.
The Waterwarden, a great sentinel of green brass, wakes over the last sealed reservoir with its guard.
Carved over the shaft: KARSH SALT COMPANY. EVERY GRAIN COUNTED.
Baron Ossek’s toll-men bar the shaft. “Every grain of salt here is taxed,” he says. “So is every breath.”
The walls glitter. Faces seem to press out of the salt, and some of them blink.
White shapes peel off the salt walls, and a dead overseer in rusted plate raises his whip.
A ledger rots on a desk, its last line written in a shaking hand: THE ENGINES WILL NOT LET US LEAVE.
Glass engines stand at the lift, still guarding the mine’s payroll for a company that burned a century ago.
Shed glass carapaces crunch underfoot like broken bottles.
The brood chamber clicks and rustles: scorpions of fused glass, and the webs above them twitch.
A single vein of salt, clear as water, runs down into a hall cut like a cathedral.
The Salt Duke sits on a throne cut from a single crystal, two barons kneeling and his engine at his back.
Sand pours in a thin stream from a crack in the dome, as it must have for centuries.
Khan Turaq’s riders have camped in the reading room. His hounds catch fire as they rise.
Every book here has crumbled to dust, except one, chained shut, which is warm to the touch.
The dust on the floor lifts into whirling shapes, and the shelves pour out beetles.
Scratched into a cell wall: WE CAME TO READ THE FIRE’S NAME. WE SHOULD NOT HAVE.
A librarian-sorcerer of the dune tribes has raised the old scholars to guard his finds.
The atrium’s mosaic shows a king holding up the sun. Someone has gouged out his face.
Manticores nest in the collapsed atrium, among the bones of every scholar who came before.
Sand fills these halls to the knee, and something moves under it, slow and patient.
The archive floor heaves: burrowers rise from the sand that fills it, and a wrapped curator follows.
A brass placard: HERE IS KEPT WHAT MAY NOT BE COPIED. THE KEEPER ANSWERS FOR IT.
The Keeper of the Last Shelf, a dead khan bound to the archive, rises with his honour guard and his scribes.
The arch is built of skulls, every one turned to watch whoever passes.
The Ossuary Lord rattles his crown of knucklebones. “Kneel, and be counted with the rest.”
Bones are stacked by kind and size, and labelled, in a script no living scholar reads.
Engines of stacked skulls unfold from the walls of the counting hall, and the ash-dead shamble in behind them.
Incense still burns in one niche. No one has lit it in a thousand years.
The wrapped priests of the bone-court rise from their niches, and a sun mage chants them on.
A shaft drops away into dark. Something below scrapes against its walls.
Something long and many-legged unwinds from the ossuary’s central well, and then another.
Broken chains as thick as a man’s arm hang from a pillar of skulls.
Chimeras chained to a pillar of skulls break their chains when they see the party.
Two thrones of bone face the door. The court before them kneels, and has knelt a very long time.
The Bone Regent and his twin sit among their dead court, a sun mage and a wrapped priest behind the thrones.
The doors are melted gold, run and set like wax. The heat of the burning is still in them.
The Sun King’s first gate is held by his chosen, still standing in the same ranks they burned in.
The floor shows the world before the fire: rivers, forests, cities. It is hard to look at.
The Glass Wyrm uncoils from the mosaic floor, its scales ringing like a struck bell.
The walls are scorched in the shape of great striding figures.
Two colossi turn their smoking heads toward the party, and the walls shake with their first step.
Iron collars hang on the walls, each one big enough to ring a man’s waist.
The kennels of the Sun King: a furnace-breathing beast, its dead keeper, and a champion sent to fetch it.
The dead courtiers turn their heads as one as the party enters, and then turn back.
The Sun King’s chosen, the last of his court, rise from their knees to bar his door.
At the heart of the tomb it is as bright as midday, and the light has no source.
The Sun King rises from his throne of melted gold. “I burned the world once,” he says. “I can light it again.”
Harrowmere. The town drowned in ash and was never dug out. Doors hang open on every street, and something has been nesting in the houses.
The Warden's Tower rises six floors over the rooftops. Its doors are bricked shut from inside. Lastward's old men say the sewers run under its cellar.
A chapel of the Lady. Her statue was pulled down long ago, and the bound dead kneel where it stood.
The sewer works. A grate stands open in the floor, and the stink of the tunnels comes up through it.
A strongbox under the guildhall's floor, its ledger rotted to a black cake.
A dry corner with one way in, out of the wind and the water. The party could rest here.
The door bars from inside, and nothing has scratched at it in a long while. A place to camp.
Old bedrolls and a cold fire ring: someone rested here before, and lived to leave.
A quiet nook, easy to watch. A safe place to rest.

The door bars from inside, and nothing has scratched at it in a long while. A place to camp.
Old bedrolls and a cold fire ring: someone rested here before, and lived to leave.
The sewers of Harrowmere: brick tunnels a man can walk upright in, and black water to the ankle.
A settling cistern ahead. The drowned dead stand in it up to their waists, waiting.
A quiet nook, easy to watch. A safe place to rest.

The door bars from inside, and nothing has scratched at it in a long while. A place to camp.

The tunnels double back on themselves here, falling a few feet at each turn toward the old outfalls.
A pump room, its great wheel seized with rust. It is dry, and the door bars from inside.
A quiet nook, easy to watch. A safe place to rest.

A dry corner with one way in, out of the wind and the water. The party could rest here.
The Warden's Cistern: a vaulted hall of black water under the tower. Things larger than men move in it.
A dry brick loft above the water line. Someone has slept here, and lately.
A shaft climbs from here into the Warden's Tower: the only way in.
The door bars from inside, and nothing has scratched at it in a long while. A place to camp.

The tower's cellar shaft opens on a guardroom floor. Arrow slits look in on every passage, and the bound still man them.
Old bedrolls and a cold fire ring: someone rested here before, and lived to leave.
A quiet nook, easy to watch. A safe place to rest.
A dry corner with one way in, out of the wind and the water. The party could rest here.

garrisons.text: Orc veterans in the Warden's grey hold the stair up. "Watchword," says the nearest, and lowers her blade.

specials.text: Bunks for a hundred, made tight. The bound sleep in shifts, as ordered.
The door bars from inside, and nothing has scratched at it in a long while. A place to camp.
Old bedrolls and a cold fire ring: someone rested here before, and lived to leave.
A quiet nook, easy to watch. A safe place to rest.

garrisons.text: Two bound lieutenants and their sergeants bar the stair. They have drilled for this every day for twenty years.

specials.text: The Warden held court here. Petitions are nailed to the pillars, the newest twenty years old.
A dry corner with one way in, out of the wind and the water. The party could rest here.
The door bars from inside, and nothing has scratched at it in a long while. A place to camp.

garrisons.text: The Warden's marshal waits at the foot of the stair with his guard.

specials.text: The floor here is laid in slow-turning rings. Walk carefully.
Old bedrolls and a cold fire ring: someone rested here before, and lived to leave.
A quiet nook, easy to watch. A safe place to rest.
A dry corner with one way in, out of the wind and the water. The party could rest here.

garrisons.text: The Warden's chaplain and three lieutenants kneel at the stair. They rise as one.

specials.text: The lamps on this floor were put out on purpose, and the dark has thickened with the years.
The door bars from inside, and nothing has scratched at it in a long while. A place to camp.
Old bedrolls and a cold fire ring: someone rested here before, and lived to leave.
A quiet nook, easy to watch. A safe place to rest.

garrisons.text: Two champions of the old war stand before the last stair, a wizard behind them.

specials.text: The Warden's crown chamber. He sealed the vale on the Dark Lord's word, and twenty years on he keeps it sealed.
A dry corner with one way in, out of the wind and the water. The party could rest here.
The door bars from inside, and nothing has scratched at it in a long while. A place to camp.
Old bedrolls and a cold fire ring: someone rested here before, and lived to leave.

garrisons.text: The Warden's last guard stands at his door: a champion and an iron golem.
The Warden's household turns from the window. Their master does not.
